ANGAD AULAKH: It really started with a lifelong obsession with space and the idea that we are not alone in the universe. It’s one of the most compelling ideas for storytellers and people in general. When we look at how short our lives are, how small Earth is and how vast the universe is, the possibilities for what’s out there are so exciting. It’s the idea that we might not even be asking the right questions yet. We don’t know which questions to ask because there are concepts so grand and profound. Exploring them through storytelling felt like a wonderful opportunity.

With short films, you have more leeway to be a little avant-garde. I often liken short films to haikus, while features are full-fledged novels. So I wanted to focus on the emotion, the moment, the visuals and the wonder of space. Technology has evolved so much that it’s why we can make a film like this on our budget today.

I’m happy to say we didn’t use any AI on the film. I’m not throwing shade at AI, by any means, but I know it’s a big part of the conversation right now. It started with looking up at the stars and wondering what’s out there and what stories I could explore in the vastness of space.

DEADLINE: Guy, I read that the two of you have partnered on several projects. Is this one the most ethereal? When you heard about the idea, what went through your mind? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

GUY KENT: I was thrilled because I also have a lifelong fascination with space and our place in [the cosmos]. As Angad said, we have so many questions and no answers. Finding some faith that there’s meaning despite not having the answers is profound to me. When this idea came up, it was an exciting adventure to embark on.

Angad and I have been deliberate about budget and scope, especially with short films. We prioritize quality and want to understand what we can and can’t achieve. With this film, the next question was, “How are we going to pull this off? How do we make it feel like the work we want to do, while making sure it works, resonates and lets the emotional moments land?”

Our pre-production work and the team we’ve worked with in the past gave us a built-in shorthand. That was especially true with our cinematographer, but finding a stage where we could create a set and build on it was also a huge part of making this feasible.

DEADLINE: The short film rests on you, Guy. You have a lot of scenes on your own. Your character is not only lost in space, but lost to himself, or somewhere in between. How did the two of you work on that story? What would you like audiences to think about through that juxtaposition?

KENT: Angad and I had a lot of discussions that began with isolation. Isolation isn’t something you show; it’s something you sit in. It’s revealing to see what happens when all distractions are removed and there’s no barrier between you and your own thoughts.

For Freddie, there’s a chance to find himself again. He’s an astronaut trained for crisis, someone who understands how to solve most of the problems he faces. Here, he’s confronted with something very personal and existential that he has no answers for.

It would be interesting if audiences were left wondering not only how they would react to meeting something beyond Earth, but also considering the hope that there’s something greater. As Angad said, even if we don’t have answers to these questions, there can be meaning in an unknowable answer. That makes you feel found in a way.

DEADLINE: Angad, what was the hardest thing about putting this story together?

AULAKH: The biggest challenge was looking at short films as a whole and thinking about how much time we had and how long the film would be. There are practical considerations, too. A lot of festivals won’t accept a short film longer than 15 minutes.

AULAKH: There are practical considerations around the film’s life after it’s released, but audiences also expect a short film to be short. Ideally, you’re not making a 30- or 40-minute short, because then you might as well make a feature. We had to think about the real estate available to us and the most effective way to make audiences leave having felt something and gone on an emotional experience. That’s what I’m interested in as a filmmaker: moving people. A big part of that is considering how the music, sound design, performance and production design work together to convey something cinematic and effective.

You also want to tell a compelling story. Weaving Freddie’s journey into a cohesive narrative in 15 minutes was always going to be a challenge, but I’m pleased with how it turned out. We focused on the emotion and on the fact that a mission has gone wrong. This astronaut is either going to be killed aboard the spacecraft or find his way home. I hoped the quieter moments would sustain the audience because they’d want to stick around to see whether Freddie makes it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: Let’s talk about the scope of the film. The cinematography is great. Why black and white as your color scheme?

AULAKH: German Expressionism was on my mind as I wrote the screenplay and thought about the aesthetic I wanted. The other reason is that we don’t see many black-and-white films set in space or black-and-white science-fiction films. More than anything, I think it looks gorgeous on screen. The light on the set, shining through the top grates, was beautiful.

We had scouted locations beforehand, so we knew what the set would look like. But the first image that came to mind was Freddie Ballard lying on the floor, screaming and tumbling. I saw it in black and white. I hadn’t shot a black-and-white film since film school, and I thought this was the perfect opportunity. The stars look beautiful in black and white. There was also a practical reason. Black and white is more forgiving when you don’t have a huge budget for production design. You can hide things in the shadows, and it worked well with our special effects and the 3D modeling. We also made sequences in Unreal Engine with Stuart Lippincott, who’s an absolute genius. His work was a huge inspiration to me. I thought the lighting, images, and compositions would be tremendous in black and white.

KENT: On an emotional level, I think black and white subconsciously creates a sense of melancholy. That’s the basis of German Expressionism, at least in my experience. There’s an emotional texture it brings.

AULAKH: Yeah, it’s very melancholic. Black and white also has inherent cinematic associations. Audiences think of films from the 1930s and ’40s, most of which were made in black and white. I love the idea that Aurora can feel like a product of the past, something you might have seen in those bygone eras. That was exciting because retro-futurism, which is used extensively in science-fiction films and video games, is powerful and interesting. I gravitate toward it, so I loved being able to use that aesthetic in Aurora .

DEADLINE: What were the biggest technical challenges, and where did you have to get especially inventive? You’ve talked about using black and white, but is there another example? How did you get inventive with the production design?

AULAKH: A lot of the credit goes to our visual effects artist, Ian Mills Miller. The entity you see in the film was originally going to be an actor, Ethan [Daniel Corbett], wearing a latex bodysuit. We were going to use his movements and digitally map them onto a being, the way they did with Gollum in The Lord of the Rings . Instead, we used Ethan as a reference, and Ian created the magnificent 3D being you see in the film.

That’s a hard shot to pull off because it’s expensive and time-consuming, and you have to be careful about how much you show. Black and white allowed us to hide the entity in the shadows. He’s a being of light at the end of the film, but throughout it he looks dark and mechanical. He’s influenced more by machinery than by alien life.

It was tricky. Having the ability to hide him in the shadows and take a less-is-more approach was effective. If you hold an effects shot too long, the audience may start to look at it differently. Even in major motion pictures, it can be disconcerting and create an uncanny valley effect. We wanted to avoid that with our digital effects.

DEADLINE: Talk a bit about your experience on the film festival circuit. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

AULAKH: I’ll take the first part, and Guy can talk about where we’ve been and what’s coming up. We premiered at HollyShorts this August, which was a lovely experience. I’m a small-town kid from Mountaintop, Pennsylvania. We didn’t have a movie theater in town, and we still don’t. Getting to screen a film at the historic Grauman's Chinese Theatre was an honor.

The festival was so well put together, and the audience response was wonderful. There were events throughout the week, so you had a chance to meet other filmmakers and talk with people watching your film. As a filmmaker, you get real-time feedback from the room. Unfortunately, we can’t attend many festivals because they’re all over the world. The few opportunities we get to sit with an audience and see the film on the big screen are phenomenal. It’s been wonderful so far. Our last few shorts had great festival runs, and we hope Aurora will top both of them. We’re just getting started. Guy can tell you more about where we’re headed next.

KENT: We’re going to FilmQuest. We are nominated for Best Sci-Fi Short and Best Visual Effects, which is fantastic. We’re thrilled to be part of that festival and what it represents. They’ve been wonderful. We’ve also done Anomaly Film Festival and Toronto Arthouse, and we’re going to Festival of Fantastic Films in the U.K. We have some other festivals to be announced toward the end of the year and early next year.

The greatest thing, as Angad said, is connecting with audiences and getting the film’s message out there. I think it’s a special piece, and there’s more to this world that we hope to build beyond the short. The more audiences see it, the more we’ll be able to go down that road.

AULAKH: We’re developing a television series based on Aurora and its world. If we can build some excitement throughout the festival circuit, it’ll make getting the series off the ground that much easier. We hope people respond to the film. After the festival circuit, we’ll release it online; we’re working on distribution for that, too.

These festival runs can last upwards of a year and a half, if you’re lucky. We’re excited to get the film out there around the world, and it has officially gone international. Sometimes things can go right in life, and this is luckily one of those situations. I don’t want to knock on wood as I say that. We’re thrilled and honored to be selected.

articles.title: Stephen Colbert Signs With UTA
articles.summary: The former ‘Late Show’ host and current ‘Lord of the Rings’ writer will be represented by the Beverly Hills-based talent agency.
articles.content:
Stephen Colbert has signed with UTA as he explores opportunities after The Late Show concluded earlier this year, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

UTA will be representing the 13-time Emmy winner as well as his production company, Spartina Industries, across film, television, publishing work and more.

"We are thrilled to be working with Stephen Colbert. He is an exceptionally talented artist and creator, a dedicated philanthropist and a terrific person,” UTA president of filmed entertainment Matt Rice and managing partners Jay Gassner and Julien Thuan said in a joint statement. “We look forward to partnering with Stephen and Spartina Industries to support and further expand his creative endeavors."

Colbert signed off from The Late Show in May after hosting the late-night series, which became a casualty of the Paramount-Skydance merger , for a decade. In the process, the comedian — who also wrote on and executive produced the series — collected several of his many Emmys as well as a Peabody Award.

Prior to his tenure at The Late Show , Colbert hosted, wrote and produced Comedy Central’s satire news program The Colbert Report for nine years and wrote and served as a correspondent on The Daily Show for seven years.

And Colbert is keeping busy post- Late Show . Currently, he’s co-writing the next Lord of the Rings movie with veteran LOTR screenwriter Philippa Boyens and his son Peter McGee, as well as working on his screenwriting software company Scripto. In a recent interview with THR , Colbert said he has been entertaining other opportunities but hasn’t landed on one yet. “There’s some fun stuff to think about. I’m in no hurry,” he said.

His production company, Spartina Industries, is currently developing a TV adaptation of Roger Zelazny’s sci-fi book series The Chronicles of Amber with The Walking Dead co-creator Robert Kirkman’s Skybound Entertainment. The company, headed up by Carrie Byalick, previously produced two seasons of the late-night show After Midnight on CBS.

Colbert continues to be managed by James Baby Doll Dixon at Dixon Talent, Inc. and represented by Tom Hansen and Don Steele at Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman.

articles.title: 'Birthright,' About Differing Attitudes on Israel, Set For Broadway
articles.summary: The play follows seven friends through 18 years, starting just after their Birthright trip to Israel.
articles.content:
Birthright, a play by Tony Award winner Jonathan Spector examining differing views about Israel among Jewish-American friends, will move to Broadway this spring.

The play is set for a 20-week run at Broadway’s Hudson Theatre starting Feb. 23, 2027, ahead of a March 15 opening night. It moves to Broadway after a sold-out and critically acclaimed run at the Off-Broadway MCC Theater this past summer. Teddy Bergman directs, making his Broadway debut after helming the Off-Broadway run.

Casting for the Broadway run has not yet been announced.

The play follows seven friends through 18 years, starting just after their Birthright trip to Israel in 2006, tracking their differing and changing attitudes on Israel as well as changes within their own lives. Spector returns to Broadway after last season’s Eureka Day, which won the Tony Award for best revival of a play, and centered on a school board dealing with select parents who did not want to vaccinate their kids.

“Just over two years ago, I was racing to finish a first draft of Birthright before starting rehearsals for Eureka Day at MTC. I could never have fathomed that such a short time later we’d be bringing it to Broadway, when the questions the play is wrestling with still feel so close to our present moment. Writing this was the scariest thing I’ve ever attempted to do, and (perhaps not coincidentally), has become the most meaningful and rewarding. I’m beyond thrilled that a wider audience will have a chance to encounter the play and see the work of our brilliant artistic collaborators,” Spector said.

After seven seasons of Riverdale on The CW and four seasons of The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina on Netflix, fans may have thought that the modern TV takes on Archie […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Disney+ has confirmed the cast for the Afterlife With Archie TV series, and it means the R-Rated comic adaptation is getting even closer to reality. After seven seasons of Riverdale on The CW and four seasons of The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina on Netflix, fans may have thought that the modern TV takes on Archie had hit their ceiling. Despite this, Disney, of all places, confirmed that the horror-themed comic series Afterlife With Archie had been given a series order on Disney+ , and now the new versions of the main cast have been confirmed.

In a new report on Deadline , the casting for Afterlife With Archie has been confirmed, with a slew of newcomers taking on the parts. Vasco Faria of Your Fault: London will take on the titular role of Archie, now caught between the life-and-death stakes of a zombie invasion and navigating the choice between Betty and Veronica. Sarah Abbott ( The Body ) and Aliyah Mastin ( Paradise ) will take on those respective roles from the pages of Archie comics, with Angel Rivera ( Escape from Mr. Lemoncello’s Library ) confirmed as the new Jughead Jones; and Chloe Avakian ( Devil in Disguise: John Wayne Gacy ) as the new Sabrina Spellman.

Meet Riverdale's newest residents. #AfterlifewithArchie pic.twitter.com/RRZ2m3Msab

The new Afterlife With Archie TV series is in good hands from the jump, with creator Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa bringing it to life in live-action. Previously, not only did Aguirre-Sacasa help shepherd the characters back to prominence with both Riverdale and Chilling Adventures of Sabrina , but he also penned the original Afterlife With Archie comic book series .

It could be argued that the Afterlife With Archie comics, which put a grim horror lens on top of the ever-pleasant Riverdale setting, is what helped revive the idea of the characters in mainstream pop culture. Not only were the comics really popular, but it ended up being what gave Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa the keys to the kingdom, acting as chief creative officer for Archie Comics.

The most surprising thing about Disney+ being the home for a live-action Afterlife With Archie TV series is twofold: the first being that the source material does not shy away from grim violence in the slightest. Recent years have shown that Disney is less squimish about mature material being on the streaming platform than when it first launched, but Afterlife With Archie isn't shy on gory details. As for the second, comic readers will know well that the series itself simply stopped, ending on a cliffhanger, with no new issues released since Issue #10 arrived over a decade ago.

In that regard, the good news for comic readers is that the Afterlife With Archie TV series may well adapt all of the released material quite quickly, propelling the story beyond what was published and finally offering some closure for a story that appeared to be abandoned. That said, it's still a major question mark about how gross this show can really get when it will be advertised alongside the likes of Mickey Mouse Clubhouse and even Percy Jackson . At the very least, a live-action recreation of the comic's iconic zombie Jughead image will be striking promotional material one day.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel Had More Trump Jokes, But I Didn’t See The CMAs Jokes Coming
articles.summary: Sorry to anyone named Luke.
articles.content:
If you’ve been watching Jimmy Kimmel Live ! – or if not live on social media – you should know commentary on President Trump and the White House in general has become an almost nightly occurrence. There’s a lot of history behind the contention, from Kimmel’s pointed jokes , to Trump and the White House’s bold insults , and FCC involvement in between. So, a Trump segment on late night? Not unexpected. Random shots thrown at the CMAs? A bit more surprising.

Last night Kimmel did spend a fair chunk of his monologue focusing on President Trump and Trump's recent visit to China. Though he made some comments about Communism, the weirdest thing he noticed about the visit was that the President seems to be wearing makeup on his hands these days to give him a little more youthful vigor.

The Trump bit went on for a while in more traditional Jimmy Kimmel Live! style, and we'll have to wait and see if the President responds . Still, I was more amused this week by Kimmel trying to get in on the CMAs commentary. Let's get into the bobsledding joke, shall we?

OK, maybe I shouldn’t have been as surprised as I was to see Kimmel commenting on country music given the CMAs aired on ABC with a big, splashy Taylor Swift appearance (that led to some Swiftie theories ). That's his own network, and it's nice to see him playing ball, even if some rumors have called his relationship with the network "unmanageable. "

That last bit is a Willie Nelson joke, which is quite funny, but only if you already know the Lifetime Achievement Award is named for him. I did not see it coming though when Kimmel brought up bobsledding in regards to “Choosin' Texas.”

Yeah, that’s a joke, but it’s also just the kind of absurd fact that’s worth remarking on. Ella Langley's crushing it, and this milestone is cool, but now I'll never think of it without also thinking of Olympics bobsledding . Sure, these are some fairly light jokes compared to his Trump stuff, but please don't say Mr. Kimmel never did anything for pop culture.

articles.title: Imax Inks Largest Cinema Deal In U.K. For New Locations
articles.summary: The agreement for U.K. and European theater locations with Moshe “Mooky” Greidinger's Showcase Cinemas gets Imax back in business with the former Cineworld Group CEO.
articles.content:
Imax is back in business with former Cineworld Group CEO Moshe “Mooky” Greidinger after signing a deal for 13 new laser projection systems at 12 theaters in the Showcase Cinemas circuit in the U.K. and Europe.

Terms of the agreement were not disclosed, but Imax has signed its first deal with Showcase Cinemas, but also with a longtime business partner. “I’ve been in the Imax business for decades and the value of its technology, brand, and strategic partnership to exhibitors have grown exponentially in that time,” Greidinger said in a statement after his recent acquisition of the 16-venue Showcase Cinemas circuit from Skydance.

“There is no doubt that Imax plays a significant role in the results of the industry and I am sure it will continue to grow and attract new audience and become even more significant in the coming years. I look forward to working with Rich and his team and making the Imax Experience a cornerstone of the new Showcase Cinemas in the UK,” he added.

The new laser projection systems will go in 12 UK locations and another in Europe. Regal owner Cineworld in 2023 emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceeding in the U.S. via a restructuring, with Greidinger and his management team eventually leaving the British cinema operator.

“Mooky is a visionary leader and an excellent partner who recognized the value in Imax long before our recent run of record-breaking success. We’re excited to be back in business with his team at Showcase Cinemas UK,” Richard Gelfond, CEO of Imax, said in his own statement.

Five of the new Imax locations will open across the UK in 2027, with the remaining locations to open in the next few years, Imax said. The deal also comes as Imax shows momentum in new theater signings after the release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey on its screens, and ahead of the debut of Dune: Part Three at Imax locations worldwide.

The deal announcement with Showcase Cinemas also comes a day after Imax said it had promoted Giovanni Dolci to the newly created role of chief operating officer, overseeing the company’s expanding global theater network.

articles.title: John Carpenter Confirms Involvement in Zack Snyder's Escape From New York Reboot, And in the Perfect Role
articles.summary: John Carpenter's '80s cult-classic sci-fi action film Escape From New York is getting a remake from Watchmen and Batman v Superman director Zack Snyder. Snyder is doing a re-imagining of the original film's concept, moving the timeline further ahead to the 1990s (as opposed to the '80s), with some whole new subtext about the dystopian […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google John Carpenter's '80s cult-classic sci-fi action film Escape From New York is getting a remake from Watchmen and Batman v Superman director Zack Snyder. Snyder is doing a re-imagining of the original film's concept , moving the timeline further ahead to the 1990s (as opposed to the '80s), with some whole new subtext about the dystopian version of America where New York City has been transformed into a penal colony.

In addition to teasing bits and pieces of Escape From New York 's story, Snyder has also hinted that John Carpenter is invovled with the film. Today, we're getting confirmation that Carpenter is not just invovled with Escape From New York in an advisory role, but is actually part of the crew of the film – in a perfect job slot.

John Carpenter was on Star Trek: The Next Generation alumni Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes' podcast Dropping Names , and the subject of Snyder's Escape from New York remake came up – specifically the film's score. John Carpenter made his mark on cinema with films like Halloween (1978), Escape from New York (1981), and The Thing (1982), not just because of his indie directing and creative bends on genre, but also because of the iconic scores for those films, two of which ( Halloween and EfNY ) Carpenter composed himself. So the question is: Who is composing Zack Snyder's Escape from New York ?

The answer: John Carpenter is. As the filmmaker told Spiner and Frakes (quite frankly): “I demanded to be the composer … and they’re not going to use my score, we’re going to remake the score.”

As stated, Escape from New York was one of Carpenter's earliest achievements as both a director and a composer, and proof that Halloween was no fluke. Having Carpenter back to compose the score instantly lends credibility to Snyder's remake, which is something the project definitely needs. Snyder's reputation has taken a hit after a string of frustrating projects launched through his Netflix deal. That includes the franchise non-starter Army of the Dead and a failed attempt to launch a new Star Wars-style franchise with Rebel Moon. In fact, Escape from New York has some fans on board precisely because it brings Snyder back to a grounded place: re-envisioning someone else's work , which has produced his most acclaimed films ( Dawn of the Dead, 300, Watchmen ).

With Carpenter there, literally watching every frame of the film as he composes for it, you can rest assured that Snyder will be collaborating a lot more on this film than he usually does.

Escape from New York is currently in production. No release date has been set.

articles.title: I Just Watched Santa Arnold Lift A Giant Christmas Tree. What’s It Like Doing Stunts At 79?
articles.summary: The Terminator is getting older, but apparently nobody told Santa.
articles.content:
I've accepted that Arnold Schwarzenegger can probably do things at 79 that would put me in physical therapy. Still, watching him take time from his busy 2026 movie schedule to hoist an enormous Christmas tree overhead while dressed as Santa Claus made me do a double take. The moment comes from a new Santa Schwarzenegger holiday ad, which follows the action icon through New York City in a Santa suit as he dodges the paparazzi. Somehow, he winds up helping a family load a tree onto their car. I suspect some movie magic made that lift possible, but seeing Arnold casually handle an entire evergreen is pretty funny. It also has me wondering: What's it like doing stunts at his age?

Four decades ago, Schwarzenegger swung swords and ran through jungles. I'd imagine climbing onto a horse in full costume feels a little different at 79. Of course, he wasn't about to let a serious observation about aging ruin a perfectly good joke. He quickly followed up with a line that had me laughing:

That's a pretty fantastic old-man joke. The timing is even better when you remember this is the same guy currently showing up in Amazon’s holiday commercial looking capable of bench-pressing a Christmas tree. Kimmel also commented on how muscular Schwarzenegger still is, which led to some playful back-and-forth between the two. Even the Terminator is still perfectly comfortable being the butt of his own jokes.

Schwarzenegger isn't pretending he can simply pick up where he left off in 1986, either. He's spoken about how a potential King Conan would acknowledge the character's age, with Conan having spent decades on the throne before facing a threat to his kingdom. That's an idea I can get behind. CinemaBlend has already covered his updates about possible Predator and Commando sequels , although he told Kimmel he was still waiting to see finalized scripts.

articles.title: 'Dig' Review: Amy Poehler and Mike Schur Reunite for Peacock's Likable but Underwhelming Archeology Comedy
articles.summary: Hugh Laurie co-stars as the head of a Greek antiquities dig in this 10-episode series from the 'Parks and Recreation' duo.
articles.content:
According to PsychologistWorld.com, the website most successful at gaming the Google algorithm and therefore appearing first when you search for nocturnal interpretations, dreaming about falling into a pit denotes "deep sorrow."

Perhaps it's the lingering impact of rooting for Boston sports teams in the early '90s, but Michael Schur has a fixation on pits and the consequences of falling into them that probably requires further examination. Dig The Bottom Line Can you dig it? Sure, though maybe not a lot. Airdate: Monday, November 23 Cast: Amy Poehler, Hugh Laurie, Fina Strazza, Geraldine Viswanathan, Antonia Thomas Creators: Mike Schur and Amy Poehler

More than 17 years after a poorly monitored pit supplied the inciting events for NBC's beloved Parks and Recreation , Schur gazes once more into the abyss to trigger the story behind Peacock's Dig , a comedy that might as well be called Parks and Excavation given that its ensemble is led by Parks star Amy Poehler , also a co-creator here. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV A Decade After 'Parks and Rec,' Amy Poehler Is Back on TV With 'Dig': "I Was Waiting for the Right Thing" Movies 'Steps' Review: A Stellar Voice Cast Including Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong and Bette Midler Gets Stuck in a Tortured Revisionist Fairy Tale

It's a comparison that's inevitable and will inevitably spark disappointment; Dig is a pleasantly likable comedy, but it's never hugely funny like Schur's The Good Place (and what is Hell if not a theological pit?) nor is it deeply poignant like Schur's A Man on the Inside (and what is aging if not the existential pit that comes for us all?). It's a minor disappointment. The cast is too good and the vibe too amiable to incite any real antipathy. Still, there's an ideal next gear, be it zaniness or sentiment, that Dig never finds.

Poehler plays Elise, second in command at an archeological dig site in coastal Greece. The various trenches are apparently primarily used as a summer program attracting American undergrads hoping to drink, flirt and occasionally uncover relics from a bygone civilization. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The program is supervised by renowned archeologist Neville Wycombe ( Hugh Laurie ), but he mostly makes morning announcements, absorbs the adulation of the "Ugs" and threatens to retire, only to stick around. It's Elise who makes everything function, but her short fuse and occasional notes of contempt for her young charges render her less than ideal for the top spot she craves.

Elise is slightly more comfortable around the staff, including the privileged Clare ( Antonia Thomas ), who helps curate the trinkets found by the undergraduates. Perhaps Elise's impatience with the younger characters stems from a nebulously bad first marriage — she's now in a perpetual flirtation with the neighboring town's gregarious mayor (Kayvan Novak's Stavros) — or the betrayal of former student Dylan ( Geraldine Viswanathan ), who abruptly left shortly before they were supposed to go start their own dig together five years earlier.

Now Dylan is back, determined to set things right with Elise and with Barry (Jon Pointing), a former flame now engaged to Clare.

Adding confusion and lots of pratfalls is Patty ( Fina Strazza ), a farm girl with limited social skills and an abiding love for Disney movies and mythology. Patty arrives as Neville's new assistant, one of several jobs she really isn't qualified for.

The series, based on Kate Myers' novel Excavations , probably works best as a group hang comedy about people committed to a serious pursuit that isn't always valued by the world at large — you know, a bit like Parks and Recreation . But rather than sticking to the simplicity of a setting that's basically a glorified summer camp, the series complicates things when Elise and Dylan make a discovery that leads to a mystery that turns everything upside down and forces everybody to learn very important lessons about themselves. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Some shots of pretty beaches and white plastered villages aside, most of Dig has a soundstage feeling. Even the archeological trenches themselves are artificial-looking, less than ideal given how much time we spend in them. But Dig quickly becomes more about a mystery with "Don't steal cultural treasures!" as the underpinning than about archeology in literal or even metaphorical form. Schur did far better at mystery-crafting on A Man on the Inside , especially in its first season.

The pilot, which isn't bad (none of the 10 episodes are) but is definitely clunky, introduces us to the main characters pretty much by having other people tell them things about their personalities that they presumably already know.

"I know your default setting is tough love, but please just learn to give people some grace," Neville tells Elise.

"It's like you're from a fairy tale of neglected children lost in the forest," Clare tells Dylan, whose chaotic energy is noticeable even to random baristas.

The problem is that the characters, despite their exposition-heavy introductions, are oddly fuzzy, and the performances don't always match the way the characters are described.

There's a logic to the way Elise, Clare, Dylan and Patty are constructed. They are four women on the cusp of transition. Elise, age unspecified, is wondering if she's ever going to get the opportunity to go from supporting player to the lead in her own life. Clare is 39, and she's wondering if she's ready to step out of the shadow of her mother's wealth and become a grown-up on her own terms. Dylan is 29, and she thinks it's time to develop some maturity. And Patty is 19, kept in perpetual childhood by her upbringing but ready for a lot of life milestones that more mainstream kids experienced five or 10 years earlier. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

It's very tidy, but nothing plays out that clearly. Elise is mean in the pilot, but she's softened so immediately that she just becomes a variation on Poehler's beloved Leslie (almost an anagram of "Elise") Knope, an enthusiast in a job she takes more seriously than her colleagues do. Viswanathan plays Dylan as more loosely flighty than chaotic, which gives her very little room for the taming or development that it's suggested she needs. I never quite got what Clare's personality was supposed to be, because "rich" isn't a real personality. And since Thomas doesn't project as appreciably older than Viswanathan or Strazza, the stratification of these four women, each representing a different decade on life's journey, doesn't really emerge. (I also don't understand what any of the characters do the rest of the year. But I guess I don't understand what Bill Murray's Trapper does when he isn't counseling the kids in Meatballs either. And yes, Dig is basically Meatballs with fossils.)

It's only Strazza ( Paper Girls ) who has a character with a fully discernible arc, written with enough specificity to lead to a fully developed performance. Yes, Patty is a broad and familiar type, but Strazza plays the bumbling naiveté to the hilt and, when the opportunity presents itself, Patty's desire for her first real friend group and her first chance at love let Strazza ground the entire series. It's Strazza's show, so if she annoys you — some viewers will find her too broad, though I did not — that's a problem. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Strazza is responsible for most of my laughs and most of the show's effective emotional beats. I smiled a lot at Viswanathan's inconsistently written, solidly delivered one-liners. Poehler is an entirely appealing straight-woman, and although I didn't find Elise funny, I liked the romantic charge she brought to her scenes with Novak. I appreciated how Novak takes a character who starts off cartoonish and makes him into an odd kind of leading man, one who the series only rarely positions as a leading man. I guess that title goes to Laurie, at his funniest when he treats Neville as a bloviating companion to the actor's adored run as Bertie Wooster on British TV's Jeeves and Wooster .

Greek viewers who took umbrage at the lack of Greeks in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey will have more to be irritated by here: The biggest Greek role goes to the not-even-vaguely-Greek Novak, and there's a heavy reliance on Greek stereotypes (several embodied by the far more Greek and far more amusing Jason Mantzoukas), even if they're introduced to be mocked or debunked. Even Greece itself is played primarily by Italy and Universal Studios in Hollywood. The use of real locations in Greece and Italy comes across more as a pretext for a pleasant getaway for the cast and crew than anything that truly adds authenticity.

Some people will suggest that these are mere quibbles — the inconsistently written characters, sporadic laughs and superficial mystery — and that I had to dig for them. And, surely, the most glaring problem with Dig is its inferiority to previous Schur creations. That's what you get for setting the bar high rather than low, or even somewhere subterranean. A pit, perhaps?
